summary: COSE Receipts prove properties of a Verifiable Data Structure to a verifier, enabling transparency and non-equivocation. This document defines how those proofs are packaged as COSE objects.

eli5.summary: A receipt proves an item was added to a public log, and anyone can check it.

questions: what is a verifiable data structure
subtitle: A compact, signed proof that an entry is in a transparency log, or that the log only ever grew.

tldr.problem: Transparency systems use different data structures and proof formats, which makes implementations heavy and hard to make interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: COSE Receipts are COSE_Sign1 objects whose headers carry a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) identifier and its proofs. The RFC defines three header parameters, two registries and a CBOR encoding of Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs.
tldr.outcome: Receipts give one unified envelope for different proof types. Only the RFC9162_SHA256 Merkle tree is defined here; other VDSs need their own registrations.

today: RFC 9942 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9162 for the Merkle tree and defines only the RFC9162_SHA256 structure, leaving other VDSs to future registrations.

sections.title: What a COSE Receipt Is
sections.content:
COSE Receipts are signed proofs about the state of a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) at the moment the receipt was issued. They can show that a document is in a database (proof of inclusion), that a database is append-only (proof of consistency), that a smaller set of statements is part of a larger set (proof of disclosure), or that something is not yet present (proof of non-inclusion).

Different VDSs produce different proofs, and supporting all of them separately would burden implementers and hurt interoperability. This RFC describes how to convey a VDS and its proof types in unified Enveloped COSE Structures.

Key terms: an Entry is something proofs can be derived for, a Proof Type is a property a proof demonstrates, and a Receipt is a COSE Single Signer Data Object carrying the header parameters needed to convey one or more proofs. The RFC uses the CDDL notation and the CBOR diagnostic notation (EDN) in its examples.
sections.eli5: A public guest book can be built in different ways. This RFC gives one standard kind of slip so every guest book can hand out slips that look alike.

sections.title: Three New Header Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines three COSE header parameters.

  • receipts (label 394): an array holding one or more COSE Receipts.
  • vds (label 395): the algorithm identifier of the VDS.
  • vdp (label 396): a map of Verifiable Data Structure Proofs, organized by Proof Type.

The integers that identify VDSs and proof types come from two new registries, described in the IANA section below.
sections.eli5: The slip has three labeled pockets: one for the slips themselves, one saying what kind of guest book it is, and one for the proof.

sections.title: Carrying VDSs and Proofs in CBOR
sections.content:
The design follows the conventions of COSE Keys. Different VDSs support different algorithms, and each VDS gives meaning to its own proof types, much as an EC2 key gives meaning to its own parameters. RFC9162_SHA256 (395: 1) supports inclusion proofs (-1) and consistency proofs (-2). Proof types belong to their VDS, so implementers should not expect interoperability across VDSs, and a security analysis MUST be done before migrating to a new structure.

Receipts are conveyed in the receipts header of Enveloped COSE Structures, protected or unprotected. When it is present, the verifier MUST confirm that the VDS and proofs match entries in the registries. Receipts MUST be tagged as COSE_Sign1.

For new VDSs, a profile may be needed. The payload in such a profile SHOULD be detached. A detached payload forces the verifier to recompute the root from the proof, which protects against the case where the signature checks out but the payload does not match the proof. A VDS specification MUST define how to encode its identifier and proof types and how to produce and consume them. When a specification supports several hash algorithms, each needs its own registration: this RFC defines only RFC9162_SHA256.
sections.eli5: Each kind of guest book has its own way of proving things, so a slip from one cannot be checked using another's rules. The checker must always peek at the slip's type first.

sections.title: Receipts of Inclusion
sections.content:
The VDS RFC9162_SHA256 has integer identifier 1. It is a Merkle Tree using SHA256, as described in RFC 9162. An inclusion proof is a CBOR array of tree-size, leaf-index and an inclusion-path (an array of byte strings from the leaf to the current root). If leaf_index is greater than or equal to tree_size, verification fails.

In a signed inclusion proof, the payload is the Merkle Tree root for the log at tree-size. The protected header MUST carry alg (label 1, the signature algorithm) and vds (label 395). The unprotected header carries vdp (label 396), a map with inclusion-proof (label -1), an array of byte strings.

Verification has two sequential steps. First the verifier applies the inclusion proof to the bytes of a candidate entry. If that fails, the proof is invalid; if it succeeds, the resulting root becomes the COSE_Sign1 payload. Second, the verifier checks the signature. Success confirms the entry's inclusion in the VDS.
sections.eli5: To check your slip, you rebuild the book's fingerprint from your entry plus a few hints, then check the book keeper's stamp on that fingerprint.

sections.title: Receipts of Consistency
sections.content:
A consistency proof shows that a newer tree extends an older one. For RFC9162_SHA256 it is an array of tree-size-1 (the older size), tree-size-2 (the newer size) and a consistency-path. The payload is the newer Merkle Tree root, normally detached, and it corresponds to the log at tree-size-2. The headers match the inclusion case, except the proof sits under label -2.

The signature and proof are verified in order. The verifier checks the COSE_Sign1 signature first, and if that fails the consistency proof is not checked. Then the proof is checked. If this fails, the append-only property of the VDS is not assured. Implementations are recommended to return a single boolean result for Receipt verification, to reduce the chance of accepting a valid signature over an invalid consistency proof. Other VDSs may not support consistency proofs at all.
sections.eli5: This slip proves the guest book only had pages added and none torn out between yesterday's copy and today's.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Some structures and proofs leak the size of the log at the time of inclusion. If a log stores only one kind of information, that can reveal sensitive details. The RFC's example: if a transparency log only stored breach notices, a receipt for one would reveal how many earlier breaches had been recorded.

Extra header parameters can also reveal information about the transparency service or its entries. The receipt producer MUST perform a privacy analysis for all mandatory fields in profiles based on this specification.
sections.eli5: A slip that says "you are guest number 40" also tells everyone how many guests came before you, and that may be something worth keeping quiet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section points to the security considerations of RFC 9162 and RFC 9053. Beyond that:

  • A security analysis ought to confirm that the signature algorithm alg is strong enough. It is recommended to choose signature algorithms that share cryptographic components with the VDS; for example, both RFC9162_SHA256 and ES256 depend on SHA256.
  • Receipts MAY include strict validity periods, for example using the iat, nbf and exp claims of RFC 8392. The details are out of scope.
  • Receipts may need to be revocable or suspendable after issue, regardless of validity period. The details are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Use a strong stamp, maybe give slips an expiry date, and think about how to cancel a slip. This RFC leaves how to do those up to others.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Registries
sections.content:
IANA has added receipts (394), vds (395) and vdp (396) to the COSE Header Parameters registry, in the range of integer values from 256 to 65535 that uses Specification Required registration.

It also created two subregistries under Specification Required: COSE Verifiable Data Structure Algorithms and COSE Verifiable Data Structure Proofs. The initial algorithms are Reserved (0) and RFC9162_SHA256 (1, a SHA256 binary Merkle Tree). The initial proofs for VDS 1 are inclusion proofs (-1) and consistency proofs (-2), both arrays of byte strings.

Expert reviewers are advised to assign the next available positive integer for VDSs and to discourage point squatting. They are told that early allocation is permissible. They must not assign a VDS algorithm that has no matching proofs entry, or the reverse. Related registrations should have the same change controller.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps two official lists, one of guest-book kinds and one of proof kinds, and a reviewer makes sure no one grabs a number they will not use.
